title: War is reshaping LNG beyond winter | Wood Mackenzie
gist: With the Strait of Hormuz closed by Iran, the market has begun treating the 20% of global LNG supply sitting behind the straits as structurally 'interruptible', repricing reliability itself as the scarce commodity. Gastech 2026 in Bangkok produced almost no FIDs or new sales contracts because leaders cannot yet model the conflict's endgame, even as ~90 mmtpa of US LNG has taken FID in 2025-26 and another US wave looks likely by default.

insights.claim: With the Strait of Hormuz closed by Iran, the market is now treating the 20% of global LNG supply behind the straits as 'interruptible' rather than firm, because even a resumption of transits could easily be constrained again.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A fifth of global supply has effectively been reclassified as optional — permanently widens risk premia and volatility in LNG contracting and freight.
insights.quote: The market seems now to be viewing the 20% of global supply behind the straits as ‘interruptible’ – even if it does return, it could easily be constrained again, feeding market volatility and further complicating contracting decisions.
insights.locator: 1. LNG’s reliability is no longer guaranteed

insights.claim: The value of more reliable supply has increased as a direct consequence of Gulf transits being reclassified as unreliable, making deliverability a priced attribute rather than an assumption.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Expect a durable premium for non-Hormuz supply — US, Atlantic Basin and Pacific projects should command better contract terms than Gulf volumes.
insights.quote: An important consequence is that the value of more reliable supply has increased.
insights.locator: 1. LNG’s reliability is no longer guaranteed

insights.claim: The LNG market is not going back to normality any time soon, and LNG leaders attending Gastech 2026 in Bangkok seeking signs of direction amid the Middle East conflict left sorely disappointed.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The industry itself has no visibility — treat any confident LNG price forecast for 2027 with scepticism and favour optionality over directional bets.
insights.quote: But over the four days came a collective realisation that the LNG market is not going back to normality any time soon.
insights.locator: If LNG leaders went to Gastech 2026

insights.claim: An immediate concern is low European storage levels if Gulf capacity remains shut in, with the EU's Methane Emissions Regulation and sanctions on Russian LNG looming as additional complications.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: European storage trajectory is the key winter tell; regulatory and sanctions overhang further narrows the pool of deliverable cargoes.
insights.quote: low storage levels in Europe if Gulf capacity remains shut in
insights.locator: 2. The Middle East conflict is still centre of attention

insights.claim: Some of the most price-sensitive South Asian countries have been buying LNG even above US$25/mmbtu, broadly equivalent to US$150/bbl Brent, which is unexpected demand from industry partly supported by arbitrage across the oil and gas value chains.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Do not mistake current buying for price inelasticity — the bid is arbitrage-driven and will vanish when product margins normalise.
insights.quote: Some of the most price-sensitive countries in South Asia have been buying LNG even at current lofty prices (in excess of US$25/mmbtu and broadly equivalent to US$150/bbl Brent).

insights.claim: Refiners can profitably burn US$25/mmbtu LNG to generate onsite power because product margins are astronomical, with diesel selling at around US$200/bbl in Singapore.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The mechanism linking record distillate cracks to LNG demand is explicit — short LNG demand when Singapore diesel cracks compress.
insights.quote: Refiners, for example, can burn expensive LNG to generate onsite power and still make good returns because of current astronomical product margins – diesel is selling at around US$200/bbl in Singapore.

insights.claim: Current high-price LNG buying is plainly not structural demand and may prove a temporary phenomenon, so LNG has probably not yet become indispensable.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Cuts against the bullish read of resilient demand at record prices — downside risk to LNG demand forecasts built on 2026 volumes.
insights.quote: This is plainly not structural demand and may prove to be a temporary phenomenon.

insights.claim: Global LNG demand is expected to increase by 60% through 2040, but that growth depends on affordable LNG and is concentrated in price-sensitive South and Southeast Asian economies.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The long-term LNG growth case is contingent on price, not volume — sustained high prices destroy the very demand new supply is being built for.
insights.quote: Affordable LNG is essential to drive growth in demand, which we expect to increase by 60% through 2040.

insights.claim: Gastech 2026 produced only a few major announcements, in contrast to the conference's usual role as a venue for championing final investment decisions or material new sales contracts.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Deal drought is a measurable signal of strategic paralysis — expect a delayed but lumpy FID catch-up once the conflict resolves.
insights.quote: In more stable times, the conference is often an opportunity to champion final investment decisions (FIDs) or material new sales contracts.

insights.claim: Industry leaders remain in a quandary, still assessing scenarios for how the Middle East conflict plays out and some way from committing to a strategic plan and capital allocation for 2027 and beyond.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: 2027 capital allocation across the gas complex is unset — guidance risk is two-sided and company capex plans may swing sharply on geopolitical news.
insights.quote: We sense industry leaders are in a quandary, still assessing scenarios of how the conflict might play out and some way from committing to a strategic plan and capital allocation for 2027 and beyond.

insights.claim: The disconnect between today's supply crisis and tomorrow's risk of oversupply creates uncertainty for both sellers and buyers and makes pricing long-term contracts challenging.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A reusable frame for the LNG cycle: scarcity now, glut later — favours flexible, short-tenor and index-diversified structures over fixed long-dated deals.
insights.quote: The disconnect between today’s crisis and tomorrow’s risk of oversupply creates uncertainty for both sellers and buyers and makes pricing contracts challenging.

insights.claim: Buyers are cautiously returning to the market for long-term contracts, driven above all by fear of getting the timing wrong rather than by a view on price.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Fear-of-missing-the-window buying can trigger a rapid contracting wave — an early indicator for the next round of FIDs.
insights.quote: But discussions this week suggest buyers are cautiously coming back to market for long-term contracts – afraid, above all, of getting the timing wrong.

insights.claim: Just under 90 mmtpa of US LNG has taken final investment decision across 2025 and 2026, concentrating contract portfolios in single-country and Henry Hub exposure.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Portfolio concentration risk in US supply is now a recognised buyer concern — supports a premium for non-US, non-Henry-Hub-indexed volumes.
insights.quote: Just under 90 mmtpa of US LNG has taken FID in 2025 and 2026.
insights.locator: 6. The US stands ready to fill the supply gap

insights.claim: Another wave of US LNG, brownfield and perhaps even greenfield, may be inevitable largely because of the paucity of alternatives, with speed and flexibility to market leaving buyers little choice despite the concentration risks.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Structurally bullish for US Gulf Coast developers, EPC contractors and Henry Hub demand even as buyers voice diversification concerns.
insights.quote: there are early signs that another wave of US LNG – brownfield, perhaps even greenfield – may be inevitable largely because of the paucity of alternatives
insights.locator: 6. The US stands ready to fill the supply gap

insights.claim: The scale of the next US LNG wave hinges partly on how fast the Majors move elsewhere, with projects in Mozambique, Argentina, Canada, Papua New Guinea and Indonesia all advancing and sponsors confident at least some will reach FID within 12 months.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A named 12-month FID watchlist; non-US FIDs directly reduce the size of the addressable US wave, so they are a competitive signal for US developers.
insights.quote: Projects in Mozambique, Argentina, Canada, Papua New Guinea and Indonesia are all advancing. Sponsors seemed certain that at least some will hit FID within the next 12 months.
insights.locator: 7. But momentum on supply diversification is building

insights.claim: Developers are increasingly betting on floating LNG as the tool to finally unlock stranded gas that has sat undeveloped for years, especially when paired with commercial structuring and financing innovations pioneered by US developers.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: FLNG yards, converters and financiers become the enabling bottleneck for the diversification wave — a picks-and-shovels angle on stranded gas monetisation.
insights.quote: Developers are increasingly betting on floating LNG (FLNG) as the tool that finally unlocks stranded gas that's sat undeveloped for years
insights.locator: 7. But momentum on supply diversification is building

insights.claim: Buyers, governments and export credit agencies are increasingly supportive of LNG supply diversification in the name of energy security, though project-specific risks remain an obstacle for some.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: State-backed financing lowers the hurdle rate for frontier LNG projects — watch ECA commitments as a leading indicator of FID.
insights.locator: 7. But momentum on supply diversification is building

insights.claim: New-school transactional LNG contracts have eaten into the market share of old-school seller-buyer relationships over the past decade, but a world of higher risk and premium security of supply puts trust back at a premium.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A pendulum framework for LNG commercial models — a swing back to relationships would favour incumbent portfolio players over pure traders.
insights.quote: New-school transactional contracts have eaten into the market share of the old-school relationships between seller and buyer over the past decade.

insights.claim: Growing availability of free-on-board supply in the Gulf of America means some buyers will seek security in the market rather than in bilateral relationships, cutting against the expected resurgence of relationship contracting.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: FOB liquidity is a structural counterweight to relationship deals — supports continued growth in LNG trading desks and spot volumes.
insights.quote: But the growing availability of free-on-board supply in the Gulf of America means some will instead seek security in the market.

insights.claim: LNG market behaviour splits by tenor: the long-term business remains very relationship-oriented while short-term trading is ruthlessly price-driven, as one roundtable participant put it that in the short term they will kill for one cent.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Do not read short-term price aggression as a signal about long-term counterparty strategy — they are governed by different logics.
insights.quote: “the long-term business remains very relationship-oriented, but in the short term they’ll kill for one cent”

insights.claim: Careful portfolio construction that diversifies risk via geography, tenor and basis will support LNG industry growth regardless of which way the relationship-versus-transactional pendulum swings.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Three explicit diversification axes — geography, tenor and basis — give a checklist for assessing which LNG players are structurally resilient.
insights.quote: careful portfolio construction that diversifies risk via geography, tenor and basis will support the growth the industry requires
insights.locator: 9. The industry is keen to find answers
